counterexample: Vertices s, v, u; edges s->u with weight 10, s->v with weight 1, v->u with weight 1. Standard in-place Bellman-Ford relaxing edges in the order (s,v), (v,u), (s,u). After k = 1 iteration dist[u] = 2, but the smallest length of a path from s to u using at most 1 edge is 10. The lemma asserts equality with 10, so the claimed invariant fails after the first iteration, showing the inductive step 0012 cannot be valid as stated.
reasoning_summary: Steps 0003-0005 state the invariant as an equality: after k iterations dist[u] equals the minimum length over paths from s to u with at most k edges. The base case (0009-0010) is fine: for k = 0 the only node with a 0-edge path is s, and dist[s] = 0 while all other entries are infinity. Step 0011 is just the inductive assumption. Step 0012 is where the argument breaks. It only argues the '<=' direction informally ('each path goes through some incoming edge (v,u); relaxing (v,u) compares against the best <=k-edge value at v plus w(v,u)'), and it silently assumes that the dist[v] values read during the (k+1)-st pass are still the post-k-iteration values. In the standard in-place implementation the edges of one pass are scanned in an arbitrary order, so a predecessor's dist[v] may already have been improved earlier in the same pass; the value written into dist[u] can then correspond to a path with more than k+1 edges and be strictly smaller than the true minimum over <=(k+1)-edge paths. Hence the '>=' direction the equality needs is false in general, exactly the objection raised in 0014. The argument would only go through for the synchronous/DP variant where pass k+1 reads only the arrays from pass k, or if the lemma were weakened to dist[u] <= min length over <=k-edge paths (with dist[u] always the length of some real path). As written, step 0012 does not justify the stated lemma.
flaw_type: unjustified inductive step / invariant false as an equality for in-place relaxation
